title: Game 9: Capablanca–Teichmann
subtitle: Coordinate the knights and convert structural weaknesses

narration.say: Capablanca has White against Teichmann at Berlin in 1913.
White exchanges in the centre and develops the bishop to b5.
Black challenges with c5. White exchanges again, leaving Black with an isolated d-pawn.
White recaptures, and one pair of rooks is exchanged.

steps.title: Keep a knight near the central blockade

narration.say: White occupies d4. Black exchanges queens, and White recaptures with the c3-knight.
The knights work together: one occupies d4 while the other remains ready to support the central squares.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Move the knight from d4 to f5.

narration.say: White exchanges the bishop on e7 and returns the other knight to d4.
White stabilises the centre with f3. Black plays h6.
White takes h6 and advances the h-pawn. Black seeks exchanges.
The knights are exchanged. White moves the rook to d2, and Black brings the rook to h8.
White brings the rook to c2 and offers a rook exchange. Capablanca presents this as a strong continuation.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Offer the rook exchange on the c-file.

steps.title: Opposite-coloured bishops do not guarantee a draw

narration.say: White exchanges rooks. Both bishops remain, on opposite colours.
White activates the king. Black advances d4, and White exchanges the central pawn.
The kings manoeuvre while White keeps the bishop active.

steps.title: A bishop move prepares king entry

narration.say: Black returns the king to d5. White puts the bishop on g7.
Black resigns. The active king and supported pawns make the opposite-coloured bishop ending favourable to White.

steps.title: Simplify with the resulting position in mind

narration.say: White’s knights maintained central control before favourable exchanges.
The rook exchange left an ending where White could activate the king and improve the bishop.
Opposite-coloured bishops can help the defence, but they do not erase pawn weaknesses or king activity.
